lectures.text:
Now, before we can start working with Microsoft Excel, we've gotta open it up on our computer. Now, there's a few different ways for you to find and access and open up your copy of Microsoft Excel. Let's take a look at a few of them here. Now, currently I'm looking at my desktop, just nice clean desktop here. The only thing I've got accessible currently is my recycle bin. If I delete something, I can find it in the recycle bin. Well, in order for me to find Excel, I'll move down to my Taskbar, bottom of my screen, and I can go into my Start menu.

I'll give that a click and I can find Excel inside of here. Let's see, there it is right there. If I scroll down, it might be someplace else in there, but you might have quick, easy access to it, just going right to your Start menu. If you don't see it right here, a really easy way to find it, just go down to the Search bar. I'll go to Search, I'll type in Excel, and it'll find anything that can contains the word Excel within its name, whether that's the Excel application, or files that you've worked on, or whatever it might be.

Well, I'll find Excel app. If I give that a click just right there, this will launch Excel. Well, before I do that, to give me even quicker, easier access to it, I'll right-click on the Excel app, and I'm gonna have an option in there to pin it to the Start. So if I turn that on, I go back to my Start menu, I'll now have Excel right there, pinned, so I have quick, easy access to it. Or I wanna get quick, easy access off of my taskbar, put Excel right here.

Well, once again, I'll go to my Search. I'll type in Excel, there it is. I'll right-click on it, and I'll have an option to Pin to Task Bar. If I give that a click, I've now got Excel directly on my taskbar, giving me quick, easy access to launch it from here. So try it out, find Excel, go through your Search, your Start menu, pin it where you like it. Once you have it, click on it, and it'll take just a moment, but this will launch up Microsoft Excel, so we can start working.

Try it out.

So when I first open it up here, it says, hey, good morning, right? Depending on the time of day, it might show something else up there. But this is something that changes based on the version and as Microsoft pushes out updates for the Microsoft 365 version.

So first, just get yourself familiar with the backstage view. Take a look at Home, see what types of new documents you can create, blanks and other templates, see if you've got any recent documents in there, and you can take a look at the New and the Open buttons as well. Try it out.

lectures.title: Introduction to the Excel Interface
lectures.text:
So now that we've got Microsoft Excel open on our computer, let's now open up a blank workbook and become familiar with the Excel interface. Now I'm going to intentionally keep this short. Just really quickly give you a high level overview of the Excel interface. And as we continue to progress through the course, we'll dive into each of the sections as they're relevant. We'll get more information later on essentially. So first, let's open up a blank workbook.

So currently looking at the startup screen, I'm gonna make sure I'm looking underneath New and I'm gonna select the Blank workbook. I'll give that a left click. We'll give it just a moment, Excel will continue opening and give us a blank workbook that we can start with. So really quickly, the Excel interface. The top of the screen, you've got your title bar, and there's a whole mess of stuff up there. So really quickly, we've got your quick access toolbar, we got the current name of your document, we got your search bar to help you search for specific features inside of Excel, and we've got your account and your minimized, restore and close buttons.

Right below that, you've got your Excel ribbon. If you work inside of any of the Office applications, whether it's Excel, Word, Outlook, PowerPoint, Microsoft Access, any of the Office applications, you're gonna be familiar with the ribbon 'cause they all work the same way. If not, the ribbon is essentially where you're gonna find all of your features, all of your commands that you have within your Excel tool or your opened Office application. It's broken up into tabs.

So you see here, I've got Home, Insert, Draw, Page Layout, Formulas, Data Review, and so on. Each of these tabs contain various tools related to that category. So on Insert, I've got things like inserting tables, inserting illustrations, controls, charts, spark lines, and so on. If I go to Formulas, it's all about generating and maintaining formulas, whether it's mathematical formulas, look up, text-based, date-based, whatever it might be. You'll find all your information about formulas right here.

Right below the ribbon, you've got two pieces. You've got your name box and your formula bar. Again, as we continue to progress through the course, we'll talk about both of these elements. The name box, very special little feature, allows you to name elements within your Excel environment. The formula bar is where you can maintain and create or edit your formulas as you work inside of your Excel documents. Directly below that kind of the bulk of the screen, you've got your Excel workbook.

So inside Excel, you create a file, you create a workbook. You give that workbook a name, that's where you store your data. Now an Excel workbook contains worksheets. It could have one worksheet, it could have loads of Excel worksheets. Here currently, I've got a single sheet in there, just called Sheet1. But I can have 10, 20, I could have hundreds of 'em. It's all about organizing your data and placing it on different worksheets. Now an Excel worksheet is something we're gonna dive much, much heavier into as we continue here, but you can see that it's broken up into columns and rows, and each of these little rectangles is a cell where you're gonna store data.

We'll talk more about that later on. Down at the bottom, very, very bottom of the screen, you've got what's referred to as the status bar. The status bar gives you updates about your Excel and what you're doing in there and what features you have active. As well as on the right hand side, you've got things like different views and your Zoom bar. So just really quickly, high level again, we'll dive much deeper as we continue here. This is your Excel interface.

You got your title bar, you got your ribbon, name box, formula bar, the workbook itself, and the status bar. So take a moment, pause the video, just get familiar with the Excel interface itself, especially that ribbon. Try clicking through the different tabs: Home, Insert, Draw, Data, and so on. Take a look at all the various features that you have available at your fingertips as you work inside of Excel. Try it out.

lectures.title: TIP - Hide Excel Ribbon
lectures.text:
Here's just a really quick tip, and it deals with the Excel ribbon. So once again, the ribbon is that top portion of the screen. It's broken up in the tabs, Home, Insert, Draw, Page Layout, and so on. And it's where you're gonna find all your various commands. Now the tip is it takes up quite a bit of space on the screen, right? And I need it when I need it, and you'll know that as you continue working inside of the application. Oh, when I wanna make something bold and change its color, I'll go to the Home tab, go into the Font section, and I'll perform those tasks.

If I don't need it, I can hide it. So currently I'm looking at the Home tab, and that one's currently active. If I give it a double-click, literally just double-click Home, this will collapse the ribbon. It's gone. I can still see the tabs, Home, Insert, Draw, Page Layout, and so on. And when I need something, I'll click on a tab, such as the Formula tab. It'll expand out, and I've got access to all of its tools. If I make a selection, for example, I'll go to Home, I'll hit the B button, still there, still active for me, and I can go through and select all the features that I need.

lectures.title: Understanding the Structure of an Excel Workbook
lectures.text:
All right, we've got kind of a high level understanding of the Excel interface, the quick access toolbar, the title bar, the ribbon, the formula bar, the status bar. Let's talk about the bulk of the screen a little more in depth. Let's talk about the Excel workbook. So when we first open up Excel, we were taken to the startup screen, and from there, we chose new and a blank workbook. So I've got just an Excel workbook or blank Excel workbook. I can currently see that this workbook is called Book One.

Now if you've opened up multiple workbooks, you probably got book two, book three, book four, book five, or whatever number you got there, but you got a blank workbook with the default name. Now this workbook is really where you're gonna store your data. This portion of the screen right here is really the workbook and more specifically, what I'm currently looking at within the workbook is the worksheet. So we called this out earlier, we got a single worksheet in there, sheet one.

Now directly to the right of sheet one, I've got a little plus sign. This gives me the ability, I can click that little plus sign and it'll add additional worksheets to this workbook. So you've got a single Excel workbook, right, where you're gonna store your data for the week or the month or the year, whatever it might be or maybe you're just storing specific types of data inside of that workbook. Inside the workbook, you can have multiple worksheets.

Each worksheet can contain its own relevant data. For example, maybe I deal with sales data and I keep a monthly worksheet for sales for each of those months. So sheet one becomes January sales, sheet two becomes February sales, and so on. The worksheets within the workbook are broken up in a grid. Along the top, we've got your A, B, C, right, all your alpha, just labeling those columns and down the left hand side, we got some numeric values labeling the rows.

Now this is very important 'cause this is how you're gonna reference content or locations within your Excel worksheets. So for example, if I take my mouse and just click somewhere, I'm currently inside of cell K, column K, row 11, so I'm inside of cell K11. If I click somewhere else, right, I'm currently inside of column E, row 21, or I'm inside of cell E21. Once again, become very important for us not only to be able to effectively reference content for ourselves, but also later on when we get into formulas, if I wanna run some mathematical type formulas, do some addition or subtraction, multiplication, whatever it might be, I'll reference the data by those cell references, column and row reference.

So try this out. Get your workbook open, you just gotta blank one open there from earlier, you can click around inside the cells and just note where you're currently at within that worksheet, what column are you in, what row are you in? Very important and we will dive into this much deeper as we continue not just entering data and making references to that data, but especially important when you get into formulas, mathematical or otherwise. So become familiar with the interface itself of the Excel workbook and the Excel worksheet.

lectures.title: The structure of an Excel Function
lectures.text:
In this section of the course, we're gonna take our formulas that we discussed earlier, utilizing various mathematical operators, things like addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, parentheses, exponents, the whole order of operation thing, and we're gonna take 'em a step further. We're gonna get into some built-in formulas called "Functions" inside of Excel. And that's really all a function is, it's a prebuilt formula. The nice people up at Microsoft who develop Microsoft Excel have created these functions to help us perform various calculations.

Whether it's mathematical, it's date-based, it's text-based, it's lookups, it's references, whatever it happens to be, we've got some built-in functions already done for us that we can take advantage of to perform various calculations. So I'm gonna pop my head off the screen here, and we're gonna talk a little bit about functions, and specifically, the structure of a function. So inside of Excel, we've got these predefined formulas that are already built for us that perform some type of calculation, and they're called "Excel functions."

Now an example of a function, a very common, perhaps the most common function in all of Excel, the sum function. So you recall, earlier, when we wanted to add up, we wanted to get a sum of values, a total amount from some values, we would say, "Equals this cell, plus this cell, plus this cell", and so on. Could you imagine if you've got tens, twenties, hundreds of cells that contain a value that you wanna add up? That would take forever. That formula would be huge, "This, plus this, plus this, plus this, plus this, plus this", 100,000s of times.

Well in steps the sum function. So the example here, we've got "equals", "sum", and then inside the parentheses, we've got a range, B four to B eight. I wanna sum up this range of cells. It's not B four, plus B, five plus B six, plus B seven, plus B eight, it's "Equal sum, B four through B eight", and that colon, dot dot, is your through. So the example down below, we got our bills, and I'm just summing up that range. (Instructor chuckling) So nice, so much easier, but it's all built into Excel.

Now, there are loads of different functions inside of Excel, but once you understand how to work with functions in general, it's gonna be the same. Some are gonna be a little more elaborate, but the basic building blocks are the same. So there's three parts to any Excel function. There's the equal sign, and we already know that, you wanna create a calculation, you start it with an equal sign. The next thing is the function name. Well, what do you wanna do?

Do you want a sum? Do you wanna get an average? Do you wanna find the minimum or the maximum value? Do you wanna use some "if" logic and perform various things based on a condition? What is it you wanna perform? Well, once again, the nice people at Microsoft have built several functions. As of today, there are over 400 functions built into Microsoft Excel, and they keep adding them, making them better, adding new ones, loads of functions. We're gonna talk about several of 'em in the upcoming videos, and even more as you continue to progress through this course.

So you got the equals first, second, you got the function name, and the last thing is the arguments. So inside the parentheses, the function says, "What do you want me to work with? Where's the data at that you want me to sum? Where's the data at that you want me to find an average for?" That's the argument. Where's the references? Where's the data? So there's the example, we got our equals, you got your function name sum, and then you got your arguments, B four through B eight.

These are the three basic building blocks of an Excel function. So there's also the argument window, this is a little helper window inside of Excel that will essentially assist you in building your functions, okay? You don't have to memorize 'em, you don't have to type 'em all out by hand, but this little window will give you some tips about the function and what it expects. As an example, you gain this by hitting the little FX button on the formula tab, but then it tells you what that function does, this one adds up all the numbers in a range of cells, it's your sum function, and it tells you what the arguments are.

So in this case, we got, number one is just a range of cells or values that you wanna sum up, and that's your function. But this is called your "Function arguments window", and we'll take a peek at this, as well, as we start building our calculations utilizing functions. lectures.text:

Now, styles aren't specific to Microsoft Excel. You can find styles inside of other Office applications like Microsoft Word. And for me personally, I use styles a whole lot more inside of Microsoft Word than I do inside of Excel, but I wanna make the feature available for you and really understand its benefits over utilizing just raw formatting, manual formatting.

Well, sometimes there's a little buggy thing that happens when you use non-adjacent cells.

Now, inside my Chart data range, I'm gonna delete that out and I'm gonna grab B4 to C9, so I'm getting the bills in February, but now I want to include the May, not March and April, but May. So I'm gonna hold down my Ctrl key and I'm gonna grab F4 to F9. Right, so Bills, February, Ctrl key and May. And if we look closely at our data source, I've got monthly budget B4 to C9, which is my bills in February, and then a comma for monthly budget F4 to F9.

Whoop, got it. Now, here's where the buggy element can happen. It may not happen to you, cross our fingers, but if it does, we'll show you how to fix it. So I'm gonna hit OK, and there's my chart. I've now got February, wait a minute, but I've got March and April in there, but they're blank, and I've got May. I mean, I've got those two datasets, but I've got this big gap in there. That doesn't look good, people are gonna look at that and be like, "Where's March?

Where's April?" Right, if I select the charts, I'm not seeing the data source in there like we saw earlier, well, I need to fix this, I need to get rid of these extra months. To do this, I'm gonna right click on the x-axis where I have my February, March, April, May. There, I'll go to Format Axis. It's gonna open up a window on the right-hand side, I'm gonna pop my head off the screen. Inside of here, we're gonna go into our Axis Options into the last option there.

And underneath Axis Options, we have Axis Type, which currently says Automatically selected based on the data, which is our monthly amounts there. Well, if I look closely, we got bounds of minimum of maximum going from our minimum of February 1st to our maximum of what is that? May 1st. Well, because it's a date, it's kind of filling in the blanks with that minimum and maximum. To change this, rather than rely on the data itself and letting Excel interpret that, I'm gonna change this to a Text axis.

This will remove that minimum to maximum and give me just the two months, I'm gonna close the Axis window here, just the two months of data that I asked for. So not really buggy, but at first glance it appears to be buggy, but it's because of the dates that are being utilized inside those headers, which are then being utilized inside of the x-axis, but not a problem, if it happens, I'll right click, go to Format Axis, and I'll just make it a Text axis rather than relying on the date values.

So a simple little fix inside of there, but we just gotta be aware of what's happening. So if this does happen to you and you grab February and March's data, excuse me, and May's data, just go in there and tweak it, change the axis type and you'll be good to go.

lectures.title: Excel Charts - Switch Row/Column
lectures.text:
Charts are all about presenting your data effectively and visually, right? I wanna be able to just quickly glance at my chart and make some intelligent decisions upon what I see. Right now, the way my chart's set up is I'm viewing February and May, right? Getting those non-adjacent ranges of data, and I can compare the different sizes of the bars and they look pretty similar to one another. But I can see really quickly that car payment was down in February, up in May.

And that the water, no, excuse me, the phone and the candy kind of swap positions, right? And now waters or phones higher than candy. Shouldn't be that way. Candy should be higher, okay? But again, I'm making these quicker decisions and kind of processing the data based on the visuals that I see. Well, right now the data's laid out so that I see each of the bills grouped by month. You get to decide, and it's a simple button press right there. How do you wanna view the data and what's gonna help message what you want to message clearer?

Switch row columns, try it out.

lectures.title: Moving a Chart to another Worksheet
lectures.text:
Now, when we first created our chart, we just selected the data, went to Insert, and grabbed the default cluster column chart. And when we did that, Excel placed the chart on the same worksheet as the original data source, which is great. Later on when we talk about printing, we could print our data source and our chart right next to each other, maybe even on the same page. Right, and that's wonderful. But charts can take up a lotta real estate.

It might be too big to do that on one page. Maybe we want the chart to have its own page so we can make it nice and big, change the orientation of the page, you know, whatever we need to do. So I'm gonna show you how you can move the chart to another location. If I select the chart, let's grab it here, I'm just gonna grab the border of it, I'll go to the Chart Design tab, and the last option there is Move Chart. I'll select that. This opens up my Move Chart window, where I have two options: as object in, where it's currently inside the Monthly Budget, we got a little drop-down, and I can send it to other worksheets inside of this workbook.

You could create your own worksheet and put all your charts on there, right? Create a little dashboard. Or you have an option to create a new sheet, give it a name. I'll call this Monthly Budget Chart, okay? I'm gonna hit OK. It's gonna create a new sheet, and the only thing on that sheet is gonna be the chart. I'll hit OK. There's my new worksheet, Monthly Budget Chart. Maybe I'll drag it toward the end, just to put it at the end of the workbook sheets.

But it's its own little thing now. Much bigger, right? I can start bumping up my font size on things, right, 'cause now I got a little bit more real estate. That's on my Home tab. Boo, boo, boo, boo. I'll jump up my legend here, bump that up in size, right? But it's its own little worksheet where you can do whatever you like with it, okay? All your data is still back on the original worksheet, and the two are still connected. You update the original source, and your chart updates as well.

So again, that was just select the chart, go to your Chart Design tab, and you got Move Chart right there. Try it out.

A very important concept that we should cover at this point, because it deals with creating clean and effective and consistent data inside of your tables. We wanna make sure that people are inputting the correct values in any given column within your list. So we'll accomplish this by adding data validation to your Excel worksheets. We're gonna talk about importing data. So you may not just have data inside of Excel that inherently lives there and was built there, but now you want to take something external and bring that data into Excel.

lectures.title: Using Custom Sorts in an Excel List
lectures.text:
Typically, when we think of sorting data within a list, there's really three different flavors of sorting. There's alphabetical A to Z, ascending or descending, Z to A, or there's numeric formatting. You can do smallest to largest or largest to smallest. And there's date sorting where you can do a chronological order, ascending or descending. Now, there's also a fourth option. This is called custom list sorting. Let's take a look. Now, I'm still inside the same exercise file, but we're gonna move away from the Employee's list for just a moment, and I'm gonna go down to the Clothing Inventory list.

So let's go ahead and go to that second worksheet and we'll find a list. Still got the headers along the top, rows of records down below, but a list all about clothing inventory. So I've got a SKU, I've got a product line, I've got crew neck, or I have a style. I've got color, size, gender, material, warehouse, units in stock, reorder level, and unit cost all making up this list. Now the one that I wanna focus on is the size, right? Now, once again, when we think of typically sorting, we've got alphabetical, numeric, and dates.

Well, what about this one? If I sort this column by defaults, what happens? I'm gonna click into that column, Size, doesn't matter where, just as long as you're in that column. I'm gonna go back to my data tab and I'm gonna go ahead and hit the ascending quick sort button, but watch what happens. It's an alphabetical sort. So now I've got large first and then I got medium, and then I got small, and then I got extra large, extra small, extra extra large.

It did a alphabetical sort. What I'd like to do is actually get it in an ascending sort by the size. So I'd like to start with extra small, then small, then medium, then large, then extra large, and so on. So in order to do this, we have to create what's called a custom list. So this is really gonna be two parts. We gotta create the custom list and then we got to sort by that custom list. So first step, I'm gonna go back to data, and this time I'm gonna go into the big sort button.

This will open up the multi-level sort window. Inside of here, I've already got size. I'm gonna sort on the cell values, but I don't wanna do an A to Z sort. So I'm gonna hit the dropdown and I'm gonna go into custom list. This is gonna open up your custom list window. Now every copy of Microsoft Excel, you're gonna have the same features that I see right now. You're gonna have an option for new lists, which is what we're gonna use in just a moment.

And then you got days of the week, abbreviated and full names and months, abbreviated and full names. Those come default, out of the box. Now I'm gonna go to new lists. I'm gonna click into list entries, and I'm gonna create this size custom list. So I'm gonna say first it's gonna be XS, extra small. I'm gonna hit my inner key to wrap down a line. I'm gonna go ahead and hit okay again, and now I've got 'em in ascending order based on sizes, extra small, small, medium, large, extra large, and so on. So try this one out. It may not be something you're gonna do a lot of, but think about the data that you work with and is there something other than an alphabetical, numerical, or date sort that you want to apply?

If so, you create a custom list and then you can use it as your sort. Try it out.

lectures.title: Filter an Excel List Using the AutoFilter Tool
lectures.text:
So sorting an Excel list is gonna make it easier for us to find the records that we're looking for, right? Put it in alphabetical order, A to Z. Put it in numeric order, put it in chronological order for the dates, whatever it is, just to make it easier for us to find those records. Now that's great, but we still need to look through all of the data to find what we're looking for. Sorting it makes it easier, but all the other records are still there.

So now let's switch gears, and let's talk about filtering your data inside of an Excel list. Filtering the data, we specify a criteria, such as, I only wanna see employees that are in a specific location. Okay? For example, the HQ North location. That's all I wanna see. I don't care at this moment about the rest of the employees, I just want those. Of course, you care about the other employees, right? They're all important, but I only wanna see the HQ North records at this moment, 'cause that's what's important to me for this report.

So in order to run a filter, and there's several different ways to run filters, we're gonna take a look at the first one here, called the auto filter. So I'm gonna click into my list, doesn't matter where, just as long as you're in that list, I'm then gonna go back to my Data tab. And in the Sort & Filter section, just next door to the Sort buttons, there's a big funnel there. This is your filter or your auto filter. I'll give that a click. This is then gonna add little dropdowns next to each header inside of the list.

Now remember the headers are really important, 'cause now when I go to filter, I go to the location dropdown, and I can filter the list through that dropdown. Let's take a look. So I'm gonna go into Location, I'll go to the dropdown, and here we do have some sort commands. I've got some filter operations, and down below, I've got some check marks. This makes it really easy to identify the values that you want to filter for. So I'm gonna deselect all, I'll turn off that first one, and I want the HQ North, so I'll check that box.

I'm gonna hit OK, and there's all the HQ North records. Really simple, right? You identify the column that you wanna sort on. You go to the dropdown, and you're just picking the values that you want to filter for. So here it was just HQ North, and that's great. There's my handful of records, and this is pretty neat. lectures.title: Format a List as a Table
lectures.text:
So in this section we've been talking about working with Excel lists, a list is really just a set of data that's got headers along the top, kind of like what we have here on the department orders, got our headers along the top and rows of records down below. Now this is just an Excel list, but inside of Microsoft Excel we have a feature called Excel tables, and we utilize a feature called Format as Table to turn our list into a proper Excel table.

Now it's still gonna be a list. It's still gonna have headers along the top. It's still gonna have all your records down below. But by formatting it as a proper table, this will open up loads of features that aren't available to us, at least not easily available to us as a standard Excel list. So let's take a look at utilizing the format as table command and see what it gives us. So I'm gonna move over to the next worksheet. This is products. On the products worksheet, we got another list.

We got headers along the top, SKU, product name, category, unit cost, unit price and status, and then all the records down below. Now we're gonna turn this into a proper Excel table. And this is really simple to do. I'm gonna click into the list. Doesn't matter where. I'm gonna go up to my home tab. And on the home tab we have a section of tools called Styles. Inside of styles, we have an option for format as table. And I've got all sorts of formatting in there.

I've got formats where the headers change, borders get brought in. I got alternated row colors, I got lots of different colors to pick from. I got several different choices to pick from. Now at this point, all we're doing is formatting as a table. We're letting Excel know that, hey, this list, I want you to treat it as a table, which then once again gives us access to a bunch of other Excel features. Now, right now it's just picking a format. So it really doesn't matter which one you pick, it's gonna get us to the same end goal.

So I'm gonna stick on our medium and I'm gonna grab this first blue one. But you can grab whatever you like, your favorite color, what whatever catches your eye. Okay, because it really doesn't matter. I'm gonna grab the first blue, I'll hit, I'll click on it. This is gonna open up the format, or excuse me, the crate table window, where I'm gonna identify first that it's picking the correct range. So I've got A1 to F121, and I can see it's got the little marque around it.

Great. It's what I want. My table has headers, it's checked. We got our headers there. Make sure that it is checked. And I'm gonna hit, okay. So now it's formatted as a proper table. Excel recognizes this as an Excel table, and I know that, because if I click into it, I've now got a new tab at the top of the screen called table design. If I click outside the list or the table, I no longer have that tab. But if I click back into the list, table design is back.

Okay, now you can see here we've got all sorts of goodies and I wanna talk about a few of these goodies here. The first one is the table name. Now that it's formatted as a proper Excel table, we can give it a name. And this is huge. This is huge, okay? lectures.text:
Now, we're gonna switch gears a bit, we're gonna talk about a new feature that applies to both just standard Excel lists and Excel tables. We're gonna deal with duplicate records. So I'm gonna move to a different worksheet. I'm gonna go move to the Duplicates worksheet, it's just to the right of the Products worksheet. So let's hop over. Here, we've got a customer list. I got my headers along the top: CustomerID, CustomerName, Industry, City and so on, and then all my records down below.

Now this is a standard Excel list. This hasn't been formatted as a table, but the Remove Duplicates command applies to both. If I click into this list, I go to my Data tab. On the Data tab, we have Data Tools, and in there we have Remove Duplicates. If I go back to one of my tables, I'll click into there, go to my Table Design tab, and here I've got Remove Duplicates. Okay, so in this feature, you've got the best of both worlds because it works with standard Excel lists and it works with Excel tables, so total preference.

lectures.title: Introduction to Excels Function: DSUM()
lectures.text:
In this section, we're gonna take a look at Excel functions that deal with lists. We're gonna see some similarities, at least as far as the type of calculations, to things that we talked about in the 101 section, but now we're dealing with a much larger dataset and criteria. For example, I wanna run a sum on a column of data within my list or table, but I only wanna sum up where specific criteria is true. So we're gonna talk about database functions, and we'll start out with the DSUM function.

Now, I'm gonna get my head off the screen here just to give us a little more real estate. So with Excel list functions, the first one that we're gonna peek at is the DSUM function. Now, the purpose of the DSUM function is to add up a column of values based on a condition or criteria. So we're familiar with the SUM function. The SUM function really takes one argument, just a range of cells. You wanna sum something up, you wanna add up a group of values, gimme the range of cells, and I'll sum 'em up for you.

That's the SUM function. Now, the DSUM, it also adds up a range of cells or a column of cells, but it takes three arguments to get the job done. Now, the first argument is the database. It just wants to know where your data's at. Where's the list? The next thing it wants to know is the field. Now the field is in reference to the column that you want to sum up. Now, the field is a part of the database. So first, it wants to know where the data's at, database.

The next thing it wants to know is the field within that database that you want to sum. The last thing it needs to know is the criteria. Now, you wanna sum up this column, this field, but which records do you wanna sum? Well, I only wanna sum where the department is HR, something like that. Let's get an example here. So inside of this example, I've got an example of the SUM function. There we go, right here. Okay, and this SUM function is gonna take three arguments.

The first thing it wants to know is the database. So really, I'm telling it, "Hey, go grab all of this data over here from A1 down to the bottom of the list, in this case, G181." That's the database. Now, notice that I'm also including the headers inside of that database reference. That's very important. We'll see here in a moment. The next thing it wants to know is the field. Right, which of the fields do you actually want to sum up? So in this case, I'm specifying cell E1, or the OrderTotal column.

The last thing it wants to know is your criteria. Now, this is gonna tie back to the column headers because the criteria actually contains, at minimum, two bits of information. It needs to know the column header, and it has to match the column header in the database, in the list, and it needs to know the actual criteria that you're looking for inside of that column. So in this case, I'm telling the function to look for the Department column, and then to look for the Sales records, and then sum up the OrderTotal.

Right, that's your DSUM function, the database, the field that you wanna sum, and your criteria. Now, there's actually several different types of database functions built into Microsoft Excel. DSUM is just one of 'em, but we've also got DAVERAGE, DCOUNT, DCOUNTA, DCOUNT counts cells that contain numeric values, DCOUNTA counts cells that are not blank, DMAX, DMIN, and DGET. Now, in reality, and this is the beauty of these functions, once you learn one of the functions, they're set up exactly the same.

They all take the same three arguments. Where's the database? Which field do you want to calculate based on? And what's your criteria? All of 'em, DSUM, DAVERAGE, DCOUNT, DCOUNTA, and so on, set up exactly the same. So once you learn one function, such as DSUM, you're gonna know how to work with all of 'em. So let's jump in. We'll take a look at the DSUM function first, and then we'll see some examples of others and more criteria. Let's try it out.

lectures.title: Importing Multiple Text Files into Excel
lectures.text:
So we've seen how to import a single CSV file or text file. What about importing multiple CSV files in one go, right? We can repeat the process that we did earlier and manually import each one individually, or we can take advantage of the Import From Folder option, where we can select all the files that we want from a specific folder and import them all in at one time. Let's take a look. So I've opened up just a brand new Excel document. You can close the one from the prior lecture on the importing a single file.

We don't need it anymore. So to import multiple files, we're gonna go back to our Data tab, into Get Data, From File. But this time, instead of from Text/CSV, which only allows you to select one file, we're gonna go down to From Folder. So I'll select From Folder. This'll open up my Browse window. You wanna locate the folder that contains all of your exercise files. Now, it's not gonna show 'em to me here 'cause we're not actually selecting anything at this point.

We're just telling it the folder where our data or where our documents are at. So once you've located that folder, I'm gonna go ahead and hit Open. We'll give it just a moment. All right, this is gonna open up our Preview window. Now, inside that folder, we got several files, but I really only want these ones right here. We've still got the Access Database, the Excel files, the PowerPoint file that's in there, and anything else that you currently have in that folder will show up here, but we only want the CSV files.

All right, down below we've got a few operations. We've got Load and Transform, just like we had before. And we've got a new one called Combine. Now, I can utilize the Combine operation here to do what I'm about to show ya. But I wanna take you into the Transform so we can actually see what's happening there. And I wanna specify the files that we want from that folder. So I'm gonna go to Transform. We'll give it a moment. It's gonna launch up Power Query.

All right, there we go. We get a preview of all the files that are in there. So I can see we got the database in there. We got other Excel files. I've got a PowerPoint files in there. But I only want those three right there. So I'm gonna filter this list. I'm gonna go up to the name, and I'm gonna go... Well, we can actually do this a couple different ways. I can do it under Name, but Extension just caught my eye, and I really just want the CSV files.

So I'm gonna go to the dropdown here for Extension, Deselect All, and say I just want CSV. I'll hit OK. All right, there's the three files that we want, and that's it, but right now, it's just showing us the files that we have. What about the data itself? Well, on the Content column, right here, we've got this little double-headed arrow. And if I hover my mouse over that, it says Combine Files. Now, very important here, these three CSV files, they're exactly the same, exactly the same in structure, meaning they got the same headers, right, and they got the same number of headers and so on.

They're the exact same documents. The only difference is the records within that structure. One is for October, one is for November, and one is for December orders, right, so they're exactly the same. So this Combine operation is gonna go through really cleanly. If your columns were all over the place, the spelling was different, then there'd be a bit of cleanup that we would have to do. But here I'll just hit the Combine Files. We'll give it a moment.

It's thinking. It's doing its work in the background. All right, in the Combine Files window, I got a drop-down here for Sample. If I go there, I can see we got the three files. If I select 2025-10, it'll take a moment, it's gonna load that one up and show us a sample of the data. Then I can do that with each of 'em. And here I can double check the files and make sure things are aligning, such as the column headers. Well, once I'm done, I'll hit OK.

And once again, give it a moment. It's working on the magic in the background. It's gonna take all three of those files and create one combined master list. So what used to be three separate files, you can see here that I've got my Source Name column, and I can see this is the 10, the October. I keep scrolling down, there's November's, 11. And there's 12 for December. And I've got all the data for all of those files. So now that it's all combined in one go, I go up to my Home tab, Close & Load, and I'm gonna Close & Load To.

I'll create a table, and I'm gonna put it into the existing worksheet just right there. And I'll hit OK. Give it a moment once again, and it loads all that data, all three files into one master list. So cool, you don't have to import individually, copy-paste to create the the master file. It's done. It's combined it all for you. Make sure you try this one out.

lectures.title: Importing Data from Microsoft Access
lectures.text:
Let's take a look at one more import operation, this one deals with importing data from a Microsoft Access database. Now, I wanna throw out a disclaimer here. If you're working on a Mac within Excel, unfortunately, importing data from an Access database may not work for you. Microsoft Access is not available on the Mac. So, just to throw that out there, you can still watch the video, you can still work through it in the video, you're just not gonna be able to complete the operation on the Mac.

So, for the Window users, we're gonna open up a blank workbook, just a brand new Excel document. You can close the one from earlier, we don't need it, don't have to save it. So, here, I'm just gonna hop right back up to the Data tab. Like I said, all of the import operations are found in this one section. So, we got Get & Transform. Now, to pull from an Access database, I'm gonna go to Get Data, From Database, and I'm gonna select the From Microsoft Access Database.

Now, if you don't currently work inside of Access, Microsoft Access is the kind of the end-user database tool, right, pairs up really well with Microsoft Excel. But inside of a Microsoft Access database, you're gonna have various objects that make up your database experience. So, you'll have things like tables, queries, forms, reports, and macros. Those are all your basic objects that make up your Access database. Now, tables are the one that we're really concerned with because tables are where the data is stored inside of a database.

So, here, I'm inside my Exercise Files folder. I'm gonna find the Access file called CustomerOrders-01. You can see that it's an accdb file extension, it's an Access database. We're gonna select that and Import. Now, just like before, we'll give it a moment, it's launching, thinking about that data, and it gives me our Navigator window or really the preview window. lectures.text:
All right, so we've got a little bit of grouping happening inside of our pivot table. The grouping that we've applied here happened because we dragged multiple fields into the row section. And the type of grouping that's happening here is really just text-based grouping. So it sees central, multiple centrals and then underneath that central, we've got all the departments. We've got Easts, it grabs all the East records, groups 'em together, and then we drop department in there and we got it broken up by department.

Just text-based grouping. Now, there are other types of groups that we can create and a very popular one is based on dates. So I'm gonna pop my head off the screen here. Let's first, we're gonna start from scratch here. I'm gonna click into my pivot table and let's get rid of everything in there. I'm gonna drag region out, I'll drag department out and I'm gonna drag the average amount outta there. We're gonna start just from bare bones pivot table.

Now big picture here, I wanna get an order total, grand totals for orders, but I wanna break it up by dates. Specifically, we've got a shipped date column inside here. Now, for our ship date column, I want to get the order total grand total. So I'm gonna grab the order total first. I'll drag that into the value section. Alright, there's our grand total for all orders. Now I'm gonna go find the shipped dates. There we go. And I'm gonna drag that into the row section and I'll let go.

And we've now grouped it by the date. But we've actually got multiple groups happening here. You can see the first one there. We've got less than 1/4/2024. So the earliest record that we have was 1/4/2024. If I go back to my pivot source here for a moment, let's see, I'm gonna do a quick search here. Do Control F, let's see, 1/4/2024. All right, there it is. 1/4/2024. It's row number 1076. So that was the earliest ship dates that we have inside this list.

So there's a bunch of blanks in there. So where it's storing those blanks is everything that's less than 'cause a blank cell is really just a zero to a date. And that's where all of those went went. But then we got 2024 records that actually have a date and I can expand that out, I can see quarters. If I expand that out, I can see months. And if I expand that out, I can see the individual dates that make up each of those orders. So this is all happening automatically for us because we dropped a valid date into the row section of the pivot table.

Now I do wanna point out, do wanna point out, if your dates, your date columns back inside your source data, if those aren't actual dates. So Excel, it looks like a date, but to Excel, it's treating it as a text value. Well, when you do that, it'll still group it in the pivot table, but you won't get all of these groups. You won't get the expandable quarters and months and days. It'll just treat it like a text value. So you need to make sure your dates are actual date values.

We talked about that a little bit in the 101 section of this course when we inserted dates. You always wanna make sure just at a quick glance if the date value is left aligned in the cell, then it might be treating it as a text value. So we just wanna make sure they're formatted properly. If you have that happen, jump into the Q&A section of the course. Let us know what's happening in there. How come my dates aren't grouping like yours? Well, it's probably 'cause they're being formatted or seen by Excel as a text value, okay?

So we've got some date grouping in there. Now I do wanna point out there's some options that go along with this. If I click into those date values, I'm gonna go up to my analyze tab and in there you've got a group section and one of the options is a group field and it looks like it's got a little calendar next to it. So I drop that one in, and I wanna format the values that come from that field.

This will open up your format cells. I'm gonna grab currency. I'll leave the defaults. Two decimal places and negative numbers will be treated as a negative, a minus sign in front of it. I'll hit okay, and I'm gonna hit okay again. And I've now formatted all of the data. I didn't have to select a specific cell.

Instead, go to the field list, value field settings for the specific field, and format the cells there. All right, so just a little bit of formatting, right? In this case, just some currency values. We'll try out some more. But for right now, I think that's looking much better.

We've also seen that you can modify the calculation, right? I don't want a sum for my numerics, but maybe I want an average, or a minimum, or a maximum, right?

We can modify the calculation type by clicking on the field, and getting into Value Field Settings, and changing the aggregate type function. And that's great. You got the default behavior, but then you've also got the flexibility that you can modify the type of calculation. Now I wanna take the calculations a step further. I'm gonna get rid of the order total. So pause the video for a moment, and get your pivot table to look just like mine. I want the ship date inside the row section, and I want just the years and month.

I had to summarize it in a pivot table, group it appropriately, and then modify the calculation to give me the results that I'm looking for. So try this out. Drop in the order total a second time. Click on it. Value Field Settings, Show Values As, and you're gonna do the Difference From or the Percent Difference From, whatever you like. Try it out.

lectures.title: TIP - Drilling Down into PivotTable Data
lectures.text:
So I wanna show off a really quick tip here, and I love this feature. So pivot tables are all about taking detailed records. For example, our pivot source, which is 1500 records and summarizing it, grouping the data, and then summarizing it through some type of calculation. And our scenario right now, we've got it broken up by the order date, and then we're getting a sum of the sales as well as this difference. Now that's great. Love it. Imagine this, you're sitting in a meeting, you're showing off you're super snazzy, pivot table, and somebody says, "Hey, that's great, but why did we go up so much between September and October, right?

September was down from August, which was down from July, but then October we shot up, right? $7,444. Okay, a difference there. Why is that?" Well, in order for me to see the details behind that record or that summary entry, I'd have to go back to the pivot source and go look for those records. No, no, no, no. In a pivot table, we have a feature called drill down, any of the summary points. So any of these calculated points, if I double click, like I'm gonna find the $7,444 or any of them, I'll give it a double click.

This is gonna create a brand new worksheet, in this case called the Detail1. And this will give me all of the records specific to that $7,444 difference. So you can see here that they are, where's the ship date? There it is. These are all October records. 'Cause it was the October one that shot up and it's giving me all the details. It's so cool. But all you do is give one of the summarized values a double click, and it creates the new worksheet for you.

Try it out.

lectures.title: Creating PivotCharts
lectures.text:
So the whole purpose of a pivot table was to take a large set of data, in our case, 1500 records, and quickly summarize that data to get to intelligent decisions, right? Tell a story about your data and then start to make decisions based off of that summary. And this has been awesome. We've summarized it in many different ways, just clicking and dragging fields from the field list into those sections of the pivot table, grouping and summarizing.

Now I wanna take the summary a step further and create a visual chart, a pivot chart. Let's try it out. So first, just so we're all starting with the same thing, let's get rid of the months and years if you have it in there. And let's get rid of the values. Let's just start off from square one again with our pivot chart, our pivot table. So let's say I want to get a counts of orders and I wanna do it by department. So I'm gonna grab the order ID, I'll drag that into the value section.

Now we've got our overall count. We've got 1500 records, 1500 orders. Let's then grab department and put that into the row section. So now I've got that count broken up by department finance 217, HR 220, and so on. And this is awesome. And how quick was that? Again, this is why I love pivot tables, just how quick and flexible they are. Now, what I like to do is create a visual charts based off of this data. Now, if you went through the Excel 101 section, earlier on in this course, we talked all about charts, creating charts, formatting charts, and so on.

What we're gonna see here is a pivot chart, but it's really just a chart. It's a chart based off of a pivot table. Now, everything that we talked about in the 101 section is going to apply here with a slight twist. Because it's based off of a pivot chart, there will be some extra features, but everything we talked about earlier with just normal charts exactly the same. So first step, I'm gonna click into my pivot table. I'm then gonna go to my pivot table analyze tab, and we've got a pivot chart option.

Now, just really quick, FYI, if I were to go to insert, you would have all your chart options right there as well as pivot chart, okay? So if you use one of these other options, like these guys here, it's still a pivot chart. It's a pivot chart 'cause it's based off of a pivot table. So either option, I'm gonna go to pivot chart. This will open up the insert chart window, and I'm just gonna stick with the default 2D clustered column chart. So column, I'll grab the first one there and I'm gonna hit okay, and there is our chart.

How quick was that, right? You've got your summary, and now we've got the summary, but in visual form. So we got all of our departments down at the bottom. We've got our total order accounts inside of those cluster column bars. Now, this is great, but the chart is connected to the pivot table. Anything we do to the pivot table also changes the chart. So watch this. If I jump back into my field list and let's say, and now I wanna get a breakdown by year for each of these different departments and their order totals.

So I think, okay, well I'm gonna go grab the shipped dates column and I'm gonna drag that into the access section. Okay, now, just to point out, I'm gonna put this back for a moment. The access categories, that's showing up because I have the chart selected. If I click into the pivot table, it'll change back to rows. If I go back to the chart, I'm now at your categories access, okay? So it just depends on what you have selected. But I'm gonna grab the ship dates. There it is.

I'm gonna drag that down into the rows or the categories area, and I'm gonna drag it above department. I'll let go. It did change it, but it got really messy, really messy. Now this is happening because of the grouping and the dates, right? Remember we got years, months, and the actual days, the dates inside there. Well, I need to clean that up. So inside of my category or the row section, I just want years. So I'm gonna grab months, get rid of it, I'm gonna grab the ship dates, get rid of it, and I just want the years in there.

So then I got years in department and getting counts for each department for each year. So again, anything you do to the pivot table, updates the pivot chart, very cool, very flexible, right on demand. You change one changes the other. You don't have to modify both of 'em, right? What a hassle that would be. Now I can get rid of year. I'll drag that back out and get back to just my department totals for those three years, all three years included in there.

Now we're gonna talk about filters in a moment and take this even step further. But try this out. Get in, create your pivot chart based off your pivot table, and try making a change. See how one affects the other. Try it out.

sections.title: Working with Excel's Power Query Tools

lectures.title: Introduction to Excel Power Query
lectures.text:
In this section of the course, we're gonna revisit a topic that we got into earlier in this 102 section, where we talked about importing data. Now, this is gonna take us into a much deeper dive into Excel Power Query. So first, let's get my head off the screen here, and let's talk a little bit about what Power Query is and how we can take advantage of its features. So first off, Excel Power Query: at its surface, it's Excel's import tool. It allows you to connect to virtually any source out there and import data from that source into your Microsoft Excel workbooks.

Now, when you utilize this import or Power Query tool, there's actually four basic steps that you can take to work with your external data. Let's talk about 'em. So the first one is you gotta make a connection to the data source, whatever that data source happens to be, and you'll find all of these options on the Data tab inside of Microsoft Excel. So whether you're pulling data from a text file, from some web interface, from another Excel table or range, from a picture, that's pretty cool, we can read content from a picture, or from a number of other sources.

You've gotta make the connection to the data first. The second thing, once you've made that connection, we then bring it into Excel Power Query. And Power Query is its own standalone application, separate from Microsoft Excel, but we launch it utilizing Excel's Power Query or import commands. And inside of there, you have a whole slew of commands that you can work with to get the data to fit your needs, essentially transforming it to get the data you want.

So, for example, maybe I've connected to an Access database, and I'm pulling out the Customers table, but when I pull that Customers table, perhaps I don't need all of the columns. So, I'll remove columns or fields from that dataset. Perhaps I don't need all of the records. I'm only interested in a specific set of customers, maybe by country. So I'll filter the data to, once again, get the data that I need. You might create calculated columns, create data that's not currently in the dataset, in the original source, but you calculate it to create that data so you can bring it into Excel.

So once again, all sorts of tools you can use inside of Power Query to transform the data to fit your needs. The third thing that we can do is create specific types of queries through a combined operation. And we've got two different types of combined queries. We've got a merge, and we've got an append, and we'll talk more about these here in a moment. The fourth thing that we can do is, once you've connected to it, once you've transformed it to fit your needs, you then load it into your Excel workbook.

Whether that means bringing it in as an Excel table, or bringing it right to a PivotTable, or perhaps just creating a connection to the data so you have that information available to you in the background within your Excel workbook. Now, I wanna talk a little bit more about the different types of combined queries that we have inside of Excel Power Query. The first one is your append query. And we actually saw this one as we were getting into importing data.

The append query, you'll remember, allows you to connect to an external source, grab multiple datasets, completely separate datasets, and append them together to create one master list. So, for example, you may have an independent list for month one sales, and a separate list for month two sales. Now you wanna take both of those monthly sales reports and combine them into one master list. Then we can create an append query. The second type of query, and we're gonna get into this one in this section, is called a merge query, very similar to an append, but this one relies on a relationship between datasets.

So, for example, you've got an Orders table, one entity, and you've got a Customers table, a separate dataset. Now I want to create a report, but that report should hold data from both datasets. Well, I can make a connection to both datasets in Power Query, bring them in, and then merge them together through a common field. So let's see an example here. So within an append, it might look something like this. We've got customer data one, and we've got customer data two, that bottom table, top one being Argentina, bottom one being Brazil.

And then I can run an append that puts both the Argentina and Brazil records together into one single list. Now, with a merge query, we have a Customers table, it's got data all about customers, and then we've got an Orders table that has data just about the orders. Now I want to combine the two together so I can create reports. And we do this through a common field between the two datasets. So here in the Customers table, we have a customer ID that uniquely identifies each customer in that list.

But in the Orders table, we also have the customer ID to help us create the relationships between the two datasets. This way I can see customer number one has these orders, customer number two has these orders, and so on, and we can create that master list that holds both the customer data and the order information in one dataset. This way, we can create our PivotTables and our further reports all from the one master list. So we're gonna jump into Power Query, we'll create connections like we saw earlier, but then we'll get in and start transforming the data, getting it to fit our needs, removing columns, sorting, filtering, calculating, and we'll get into relationships so we can see how those are built through Excel Power Query.

All right, let's jump in.

lectures.text:
During this section of the course, we're gonna talk about a tool inside of Excel. It's an add-in tool called Excel Power Pivot. Now it is an add-in. It's something you have to activate, but even before you activate it, you gotta be working with a proper edition of Excel to get access to this add-in. Now, it's a great tool, I love it. I highly recommend it, but it is not available in every edition of Microsoft Excel. So I've got a page open in front of you.

I did a quick search online, I just typed in Excel Power Pivot, add-in, and I came up with this Microsoft page here. It is not available in every copy of Excel. So I just wanna get this outta the way because this is a question that I get asked a lot. "I've heard about Power Pivot, but when I go into my copy of Excel, I don't see it. Why do I not have access to it?" Well, Excel Power Pivot was introduced in the 2010 edition of Microsoft Excel. When Microsoft first announced it or first introduced it, it was available to that copy and all copies of Excel 2010.

When the 2013 version of the Office Suite Excel was introduced, Microsoft made some adjustments and it's now from 2013 to newer. It's not available in all copies of Microsoft Excel. So that's what this page is gonna talk about, just where is it at, what versions of Excel is it available within. Now for me personally, I go through the Office or Microsoft 365 service. This is the monthly subscription model that Microsoft has created for their Office applications.

And as you can see here, Power Pivot can be found in the following products. I'm gonna do a little bit of highlighting here. The subscription products, so it is available inside of Microsoft 365, all versions that include desktop versions of Excel for Windows. So if you are going through Microsoft 365 and you can download Excel locally to your computer as a desktop application, it is available to you there. It is also available for one time purchases, perpetual licenses, so you purchase the Excel, you download it to your computer, you purchase that application.

It's available in Office Professional 2019, Home Office 2019, Home Student 2019 and so on. And as well as 2010. Now, if you are working on 2010, I'm gonna show everybody where you can find this at, but if you get into there in 2010 and you don't see it, they do provide a free download link for you to go get that download and install it into your system. Now, where it's not included is Office Professional 2016 Home and Student 2013, Home and Student 2016 and so on.

And it is not available on the Mac release. Any copy of Microsoft Excel on a Mac, it is not available. Unfortunately, it's one of those features that just hasn't made that transition yet. Although I have been reading that there are beginnings of some features showing up inside the Mac release. We'll see how far that goes though. So just so you know, I wanna get that outta the way 'cause that's a question I get asked a lot. "Where's it at? I've opened up my copy of Excel.

I've followed your steps to go activate it, but I can't find the add-in. Where's it at?" Well, it might be based on what version of Excel you're working with. So once again, it's a great tool, highly recommend it. If you don't have a proper copy of Excel for Power Pivot, I would recommend going out and finding a copy that does contain it. It is a great tool and we're gonna see just how powerful it is. Now, I do wanna point out, if you don't have Power Pivot loaded on your system, that's okay.

It's gonna be a handful of videos that we're gonna go through here. Introducing kinda introductory level concepts that are found inside of Power Pivot. So you can still watch the videos or you can skip 'em, move on until you do have that copy that does contain Power Pivot. If you skip 'em or you don't complete the exercises, this will not hold you up in future lectures throughout this course, okay? So don't worry about that. You're taken care of there.

I haven't built anything that relies on the content in this section. Alright, with that said, let's take a look at the power that comes with Excel Power Pivot. We'll jump into the next video.

lectures.title: Using the Freeze Panes Tool
lectures.text:
In this section we're gonna talk about managing large data sets, and that's really what we've been talking about throughout this entire 102 section. But now I'm gonna give you some additional tips and tricks to make it even easier to work with those larger data sets, or to prepare larger data sets. So the first thing that we're gonna discuss here is gonna help us identify content within larger data sets. Take a look. So I'm still inside the same exercise file that we've been working with.

I'm currently in the Excel 102 ExerciseFile-01, and I'm looking at the ServiceRequests worksheet. Now, this is a pretty decent sized list. It's got a load of headers up there, from RequestID, RequestDate, CustomerName, RequestType, and so on. And it's got a few records. Now, what I really want you to pay attention here is when I scroll down inside this list, whether I'm searching for records or I'm trying to get to the bottom of the list, you'll see that our headers just zipped right off the top of that screen, right?

So RequestID and date and customer and so on, all of those headers, row 1, are gone. So I wanna make this easier to identify my headers as I'm scrolling through larger lists. Inside of Excel there's a feature called Freeze Panes. Take a look. So the first thing I'm gonna do here is identify the row that I wanna keep at the top of the page. In this case, it's row one. So I'm gonna click in the cell right below row one. I'm gonna click in the cell A2.

Now I'm gonna go to my View tab, top of the screen. Then I'm gonna go over to Freeze Panes. I'll go to Freeze Panes, and the first option in there is Freeze Panes. Now remember, I'm currently selecting cell A2. So when I select Freeze Panes here, it's gonna freeze everything above that current selected cell. So Freeze Panes, Freeze Panes. And now when I scroll down, those headers remain static at the top of my screen. This is your Freeze Panes. Now I wanna take it a step further.

If you've got a really wide list, let's say I zoom in here a little bit. And as I start scrolling to the right, so if I scroll to the right here, I lose some important information off to the left, such as the RequestID. So you ever scroll inside of Excel and put your finger on the screen, kinda trying to keep track of where you're at? Well take a look. I'm first, I'm gonna go back to View, Freeze Panes, and I'm gonna Unfreeze just for a moment, but this time I'm gonna click inside of cell B2.

Then I'm gonna go back to View, Freeze Panes. Freeze panes. Now this time, because I was in B2, it's gonna freeze everything above it. So if I scroll down, I keep the headers, but it's also gonna freeze everything to the left of it. So if I scroll to the right, that RequestID stays put. So cool, right? Freeze Panes. Try it out.

lectures.title: Grouping Data (Columns and/or Rows)
lectures.text:
When working with larger datasets, there will come a time where you wanna print out a document or just visually look at it here inside the worksheet view. But you don't need to see every column or every row. Inside of Microsoft Excel, we have a feature called Group and Outline. And this is going to allow us to group columns so that we can collapse them and expand them as needed. Take a look. So inside of this particular worksheet, I'm looking at the Service Requests worksheet.

Let's say the severity and the status, these two columns, they're great. They provide some really useful, valuable information, but I don't always need them. So rather than deleting them because it still contains useful, relevant information, I'm not gonna delete 'em, but I'll group 'em so I can collapse 'em down to hide those columns. So to do this, I'm gonna highlight columns E and F. I just clicked and dragged over the column headers E and F.

I'm gonna go to my Data tab. And on the far right we have a section in there called Outline. And then we got one called Group. I'm gonna give Group a select and I'll select Group. So that took those two columns, and now I've got this little group and outline command where I can click that little box, the minus sign, and it'll collapse those two columns, essentially just hiding them. If I hit the plus sign, this will expand them back out. Whoop, whoop, pretty cool.

This is part of your Group and Outline feature. Now, let's try it one more time here, let's say notes. I don't always need to see the notes. So I can select K. I'll go back to Data, Group, and I'll group it. So now I've got two groups up there. I can collapse the notes. I can collapse the severity and the status, or I've got these little numbers off to the left. If I hit a two, it'll expand 'em back out. If I hit a one, it'll collapse 'em both. So this is your group command.

You just select the column or columns, go to your Data tab and you got your Group command. Now if you wanna ungroup it, I no longer need the groups. I'll expand them out. I can select that E and F again, and I'll go back to Group. But I'm going to actually, I'm gonna go to Ungroup and I'm gonna ungroup those columns and I'll get rid of that Group and Outline feature. So group 'em, ungroup 'em, whatever you need, but temporarily, essentially just temporarily hiding them and then expand 'em when you need them.

lectures.text:
Oh, here we are. Welcome to the Excel 103 section, or the advanced topics found within this course. So you've just completed the Excel 102, or the intermediate topics. Now we're gonna take that knowledge that you built through 101, 102, and now bringing it up to the 103 section. We're really just building stepping stones to get us to more complex and more advanced topics inside of Microsoft Excel. So I hope you're ready for this. (graphics whooshing) I wanna introduce you to the topics before we actually jump in.

So, the first group of topics that we're gonna get into is gonna be about conditional functions or logic-based functions. We're gonna talk about things such as the IF function. We're gonna talk about the SUMIF. If I wanna SUM up a range of cells, IF this is true. Or the COUNT function, I want to count to group of cells, but only if this specific criteria is true. So, all about these logical statements that perform some form of a calculation, but based on a condition.

Then we're gonna talk about name ranges. Inside of the 101 section, we started talking about Excel absolute references, really identifying and using the relative and absolute references, and why you would do that in different situations for each. Now we're gonna take absolute references to the next level. We're gonna talk about named ranges. And name range essentially gives you the option to name a cell or group of cells. So rather than referencing a cell by its column and row reference, most common way, we'll talk about how you can name that range, and then utilize the name to reference the content.

Then we're gonna talk about nesting functions. So, the ability to take one function and place it inside of another Excel function to get it to do more for us. So, where one function just isn't enough, will nest another function in there to help it out and get it to become more robust and more dynamic for us. Then we're gonna talk about perhaps one of the most popular, more advanced functions, we're gonna get into Excel LOOKUP functions. Specifically, we'll talk about the VLOOKUP.

A very, very popular function. So it gives us the ability to look up a value from a master list, and then pull related data from that list based on the initial value. We'll also talk about the INDEX and MATCH functions because the VLOOKUP has some limitations, and we're gonna overcome those limitations by utilizing a pair of functions, INDEX and MATCH. Then we're gonna talk about Excel text-based functions. Essentially functions like LEFT, RIGHT, MID, SEARCH, LEN, CONCAT, all these functions that work with text values.

So, we've been doing a lot of calculations like mathematical stuff, but now we'll see how to run calculations based on text values, things like names, addresses, you know, text values. Then I've got a whole section based on functions that are new to the Excel Microsoft 365 edition. So if you're a subscriber to the Microsoft 365 subscription, then you're gonna get access to some special functions that unfortunately are not available in earlier additions of Microsoft Excel.

So, if you don't have Microsoft 365, when you get to that section, you can watch the videos, you can learn about 'em, you just may not be able to work with them inside your copy of Microsoft Excel. That's just the reality of the way that Microsoft is bringing the Office applications. Then we're going to get a little bit of AI inside of Microsoft Excel, and we're gonna discuss the Copilot function. So, how we can bring AI to help us out with calculating or summarizing data inside of our Microsoft Excel datasets.

Then we're gonna talk about auditing our formulas. So, there's loads of tools that are gonna assist us in our auditing of our documents. So, we get in there and we kind of dissect the formulas and figure out why things are going wrong, highlight cells that are irrelevant for us as we work with formulas and so on. Then we're gonna talk about adding a form of protection to our data inside of Excel. We're actually gonna see three different ways to protect your data.

We'll talk about worksheet protection, we'll talk about the workbook protection, and we'll talk about adding a password to just open the document. So loads of way to really protect your content. Then we're gonna talk about a group of tools called What-If. What if this happens? Or what if this changes? Or what if I do this? How will it affect my data? We're gonna talk about a load of different What-If tools. These are pretty cool, and you're gonna see that they do a lot for you with a little bit of input from us.

Then our last topic that we're gonna get into deals with automation. We're gonna get a quick preview that's really gonna lead us into the next major section of this course, we're gonna talk about macros, how you can automate your experience inside of Microsoft Excel by recording your steps, and then later on when you wanna redo those steps, perhaps with new data, you just run your macro and it does it all for you. (tongue popping) Your mind will be blown as you get in there and see what macros can do for you, all the time it can save you just automating your experience inside of Microsoft Excel.

So, I hope excited about this section of the course. We're getting into advanced topics here. If there's something that you're still not quite clear on in the earlier sections, whether it's 101 or 102, or wherever it happens to be at, make sure you're taking advantage of the Q&A section found within this course. I'd love answering questions. I'd love hearing feedback and comments and what you're enjoying about the course. So, make sure you visit the Q&A section of the course.
