lectures.title: Advantages and Disadvantages of Excel Name Ranges
lectures.text:
Now, there's definitely advantages to utilizing an Excel named range, but there's also some disadvantages and it really comes down to your calculation and the layout of your data. Take a look. So I've moved over to the next worksheet. This one's called If Function, and we'll talk about the Excel if function here in a moment. But let's continue talking about named ranges for just a moment here. So here, I've got a simple little table that I've got sales individuals.

I've got their weekly amounts, and I wanna find the total amounts here, right? Week 1, Week 2, Week 3, and Week 4. Now, typically, and when I wanna sum these up, I'd say =SUM, I'd open up a parentheses, and I would grab the range of cells that I wanna sum up. Again, utilizing the column-row cell references. I'll close that parentheses, hit my Enter key, and boom, I've got my total. Now, way back inside the 101 section, we talked about how there's two different types of cell references.

There's relative, which is what I'm using right here. All it says is from this location, go one, two, three, four cells, five cells up, grab that range and sum it, give me the returning value, great. And this makes it really easy with a layout like this that I can then grab the autofill, drag it to the right, and it would do the same thing just based on its new relative position. So here, this is in C column, so now it's grabbing C5 to C9. Here, it's grabbing D5 to D9, and so on.

And that's great because of the layout of the data and the type of calculation that I'm copying, it works perfect. Now, if we go back to named ranges, we're gonna see a disadvantage here. Now, I deleted out my formulas. All that hard work, gone. Now, if I go back to B10, I wanna get a total here, but I'm gonna turn this range of cells into a named range. So I'll grab the Week 1 data, B5 to B9. I'll go to my little name box here, and I'm gonna call this Week1.

I'll just call it Week1. No space again, doesn't allow spaces inside your named ranges. I'll hit my Enter key and that range of cells is now called Week1. So if I drop down into B10 and I say =SUM, open parenthesis Week1, there it is, Week1, I'll hit my Tab key here to accept it, I'll close the parentheses, hit my Enter key. There's my 40,402. It's working perfect, right? But I now need to do it for Week 2, 3, 4. So if I grab the autofill and I drag it over, what's happening?

Well, each of the formulas are referencing that named range, Week1, Week1, Week1. So, I love named ranges. We definitely have a place for 'em. Like the prior example, if I go back to the Employee Commission, we had that one cell that each of these formulas needed to reference. So I give it a nice clean name, and then I can use that in the formulas. And as I drag that down, it'll keep using the relative reference as the first value C5 or C6 or C7 and so on, but it'll always go back to come to that D2 cell.

Now, with this example here, not the best example, not the best place to use it. 'Cause here, it's just gonna repeat Week1, Week1, Week1. Now, I could create a Week 2 reference. I could grab this range of cells, C5 to C9, and call this Week2. And then inside my formula, I'll just change that to Week2, and now I'm good to go. But now I'm creating one, two, three, four different cell references inside of named ranges. And I've gotta manage all of that.

And just, it's starting to create more work for me, right? So instead of named ranges, I'll just use the typical cell references in this scenario. Okay, so you've got some pros, you got some cons. You need to think about where you're using it at, right? And is it really starting to automate your work for you or is it creating more work for you? Okay, now we're gonna see some more examples of where we should use it and what would be good practice to use it.

But we can see a pretty decent-sized disadvantage here. So you could try this out. Just get a feel for it, right? Which one do you prefer? Do you like the named ranges? Or are you gonna use your cell references in this scenario, right? Try it out.

So we're gonna take the IF function that we were just talking about and we're gonna take it several steps further. But in order to get the IF function to do more for us, we're gonna introduce a concept called nesting functions. So let me pop my head off the screen here for a moment. The idea of a nested function, it's essentially taking one function and placing it in an argument of another function. So let me give you an example here. We just got done talking about the IF function and the if function takes three arguments.

It wants to know the logical tests. That's that expression. It wants to know what to do if the value is true and what to do if the value is false. So three separate arguments within the IF function. Now, very important here, the standard IF function, it's logical test argument, that first argument only allows for one logical test. That's it. In our earlier example, we just wanted to know if a monthly total was greater than or equal to a goal, 34,000.

Remember that from the prior videos? But it can only test for one thing. If you had situations where you needed to test for multiple things and then based on the results of multiple tests, then return a value if it's true and return a value if they're false, you would have to introduce another function into the logical test to get the IF to test for multiple things. So here we can utilize an and function. So in this example, I've taken the AND function and its purpose is to test multiple things using and logic.

So it'll say something like, "Hey, check this first test, test number one. Is that true? And is test number two true? And is test number three true?" You can do up to 255 tests inside of an and function. So now we're opening up the if function so much more because we can nest an and within the logical test of the if. So, this again is called nesting. We're just taking one function and placing it within an argument of another function. Let's take a look at an example.

lectures.title: Introduction to Excel Text Functions
lectures.text:
In this section of the course, we're gonna talk about Excel text-based functions. Now, before we get in and start working with these functions, let's run down the various functions that we're gonna talk about in this section. Now, when I say text-based functions, I mean text, meaning it could be straight up alpha, A to Z. It could be a mixed, alpha and numeric. Or mixed special characters with alpha and numeric. Whatever. Anything that's not classified as a straight up numeric or date value I'm gonna consider a text value.

So there's a various functions that work with alpha characters or special characters or mixed strings. The first set that we're gonna get into all relate to one another. This is the LEFT, RIGHT, and MID functions. These functions allow us to extract a set of characters, a set number of characters from position within a string of characters. So for example, if you've got a value instead of cell A1, and I just wanna extract the first three characters from the left-hand side of that cell, I could use the LEFT function.

So we'll talk about LEFT, RIGHT, and MID. The next one is the SEARCH function. This one allows you to search a value, a cell, for a specific value, and it would return its position that it found it at within that cell. The next one is the CONCAT function. This one allows you to combine multiple text values into one. So you've got multiple columns of values. Now you wanna combine all of those column values into one value. The CONCAT function will allow you to do this.

There's actually many different ways to accomplish this task inside of Excel. We'll take a look at CONCAT first, but we'll see a few others later on. We're also gonna talk about the PROPER function. There's actually three of them that we can really throw into the mix here. There's PROPER, UPPER, and LOWER, and each of 'em allow us to change the different case for a text value, whether it's proper case, lowercase, or uppercase. Then we're gonna talk about two functions closely related, but with a pretty significant difference between the two.

We've got the CLEAN function and TRIM function. The TRIM function allows us to trim out extra spaces. Like you might have leading or trailing spaces on a value within a cell. The CLEAN function allows you to remove non printable characters. Things like line breaks or the tab key. Anything that you won't see visually on the screen perhaps when you import data in, but it allows you to clean it out so that Excel works with a clean version of the value.

So all text-based functions, and we're gonna dive into each of 'em. Let's go.

Now, there's nothing in it currently, but if I go to the cell, go to the dropdown, I'm gonna pick a customer here, B's Beverages, and it'll filter for that customer.

I love this. I love this. Any way you can make something more dynamic, more intuitive, it's a win. And we've done just that. We had the FILTER function filter the results of a list. Make sure you try it out.

Here's what the xlookup's gonna do for us. I've got a simple little table, actually two beginnings of two tables here. The first one is where we're gonna focus from B4 to G4. The next function that we're gonna take a look at here is the TEXTJOIN function, another new function inside of the Microsoft 365 version of Microsoft Excel. Now, this function is gonna feel very similar to the CONCAT or the CONCATENATE function. Let's take a look. So I'm gonna move over to the TEXTJOIN FUNCTION just right next door to the SWITCH FUNCTION worksheet. And here, I've got a simple little table with an applicant ID, a first name, a last name, an empty full name, and a skill for each of these applicants.

Now, what I'd like to do is fill out the full name column. Right now, first and last name, they're two separate columns, which, typically, that's great. We want the values broken up so we can manipulate them individually, but at some point, especially when you get to reporting, full name smashed together is what you want. Now, typically I would use something like the CONCAT function or the CONCATENATE function, but Microsoft introduced this function called TEXTJOIN, which streamlines your efforts and more efficient to combine multiple text values into one.

lectures.title: Tracing Dependents in Excel Formulas
lectures.text:
Now, we've got another trace option inside of our formula auditing tools. We just took a look at Trace Precedence where we can select a formula, hit the Trace Precedence button, and it would highlight or draw arrows to the cells that the formula is using. Well, what about the opposite? What if I select a non-formula cell and I hit the Trace button, will it show me the formulas that use that cell? Well, there's a button called Trace Dependence. Take a look.

So, I'm gonna hop into my Sales Figures here and I'm gonna grab one of the cells. Let's say B5. I'll give that one a click. That's not a formula, this is just a raw numeric value, 9,550. Now, with that cell selected, I'll go back to my Formula Auditing, and I'm gonna go to Trace Dependence. So, this is gonna draw arrows to those cells that rely on the active cell, in this case, B5. So, I'm gonna click Trace Precedence, or excuse me, Trace Dependence, and it shows me, drawing an arrow.

So, it looks like this cell right here, F5, which is a sum, right, summing up that range. And this cell right here, I5, which is that Bonus Status with that big if also references that cell, and this cell right here also references that cell. So, just really quickly, I can select a non-formula cell and I'll go to my Trace Dependence and it'll draw those arrows to the formulas that rely on that cell. Now, I said non-formula, but sometimes formulas, right, are referenced by other formulas.

Let's try this. If I click into one of these YES or NO values. Let's see, I'll grab this H8 cell, and I'm gonna go up and hit the Trace Dependence. I can see that both the NO BONUS or the I8 cell and the F12 cell both rely on that H8 cell. So, if I give this number 1 a double click here, I can see it actually references H5 to H9, all of those cells, or if I go into the I8 cell, inside of there, it is referencing the H8 where that YES is coming from, or the NO, or whatever it might be.

So, again, you can select a cell and then find out what cells rely or are dependent upon the active cell. This is great if you've inherited a worksheet and you're trying to figure out what's going on inside that worksheet. You got all these formulas. "You know, what if I change this value inside of this cell, will it affect anybody else out there?" Well, utilizing the Trace Dependence will help you find those cells.

lectures.title: Protecting the Structure of a Workbook
lectures.text:
As I mentioned earlier, there's three different ways that we can protect data inside of Microsoft Excel. We just saw Worksheet Protection. Now let's take a look at Workbook Protection. So, when we did Worksheet Protection, we were really protecting cells, right? What can they edit, what can they not edit? Now, we're gonna talk about the bigger picture or the workbook, and this really deals with the structure of your workbook. Take a look. If I go back to Review, there's an option inside the Protect section called Protect Workbook.

I'm gonna go ahead and give that a click. This opens up your Protect structure in Windows, and really, it's only gonna give us one option, Structure, but we'll talk about the other. First thing, optional, although I recommend it, put in a password. So, I'll use password as my password. And then we get to tell it to protect what? In this case, the structure. You'll see that Windows is grayed out. That's an old feature. It's hanging around for legacy purposes, but that dealt with much, much earlier versions of Microsoft Excel.

In the earlier, earlier versions of Excel, when you opened up multiple workbooks, they opened up in the same instance of Microsoft Excel. Now, current versions of Excel, when you open up multiple workbooks, they open up their own instance of Microsoft Excel. So, the Windows, no longer relevant for us in modern-day Excel. But Structure, now, Structure deals with the worksheets within the workbook. By protecting the workbook and protecting the structure, users will no longer be able to delete worksheets, add worksheets, change the order of worksheets, move them around and such, or did I already say add?

Add worksheets, okay, or rename them. So, if I put in my password, I'll keep Structure active. I'll hit OK. It's gonna ask me to confirm once again. All right, so it is now protected. If I go down to a worksheet, like Worksheet Protection, I'm gonna right-click on it and you'll see, Insert, Delete, Rename, Move, Copy, Hide, Unhide. They're all grayed out. So, you can't change anything about the worksheets within the workbook. You can still edit the data, right?

As long as you haven't protected the worksheet, but you can't edit anything about the worksheet tabs. No deleting, adding, moving, copying, hiding unhiding. You can't do any of that. And that's really important, because if you have formulas that reference cells across different worksheets, you don't want users deleting things and changing the order or renaming them, right, 'cause that would potentially break your formulas. So, think about this, right?

Do I need to protect the structure of my workbook, okay, or the worksheets within that workbook? Now, we've been able to protect it, so I can't do any of those things. Later on, you, as the responsible party of this document, you now want to modify the worksheets. Well, you'll go back to Review. I'm gonna go back to Protect Workbook, but I gotta put my password in. Got my password, and if I go back down, right click, I can now Insert, Delete, and so on for my worksheets.

Now on the Goal Seek, we've got a simple little set of values. Now this is gonna introduce a new function, or at least a function we haven't talked about together, called PMT, or the payment function. Then our number of payments, or Nper, I'll grab the term amount, B4, and then the Pv, or present value, I'm gonna grab the mortgage amount, B2. lectures.text:
The next What-If tool that we're gonna take a look at here is called an Excel Data Table. Now, before we get in and start to create the Data Table, let's talk about what the Data Table's gonna do for us. So, open in front of you, I'm looking at the Data Table worksheets. This is gonna take us back to our Goal Seek discussion. First thing we have is a nice little table that tells us the terms of a potential loan. So, I've got a mortgage amount of $220,000, an interest of 8%, and term of 300 months. All right, 8%. Just crazy. All right. Now, below that, we have a data table. Now, inside of Microsoft Excel, there's two different types of data tables. We're gonna work with a single-variable data table. So, here's what it's gonna do for us.

First, this top right cell here, that's C7, contains a formula, and it's the same formula that we used earlier inside the Goal Seek. It's utilizing the Payment function, and it's taking the interest, right? That 8%, C3, dividing it by 12 to give us that annual percentage rate. Then it's giving us the C4 cell, which is the term, 300 months, and then the C2 cell, which is the principal amount, the mortgage amount of $220,000. Then it's gonna give us the results.

What is our monthly payment based off of those three values? And, in this case, $1,698. Now, what I'd like to get is a table that lists out the monthly amount for various interest rates. You know, 8%. I mean, as painful as that is, I've got that, but now I wanna see what would that value be if it was seven and a quarter percent. What would it be if it was seven and a half, or seven and three quarters, and so on. I want to get a complete table that shows us the monthly amount for each of those interest rates.

Now, an Excel Data Table, it's gonna do that for us. It's essentially gonna take this column of values and plug them into the C3 cell within this formula. Just substitute 'em in there. Oh, at seven and a quarter, you're gonna get this much. At seven and a half, you're gonna get this much, and so on. This is a data table. Now, according to Microsoft, a single-variable data table has to be set up in a very specific way. First, the first column has to be your list of variables, your list of, in this case, alternating interest rates, whatever it is that you're going to substitute into the formula.

The second column, the very first cell there needs to contain the formula that those interest rates or those variable amounts are going to substitute into; it has to be set up just like this. So, my first step to create the Data Table, I'm gonna select the table from B7 to C14, get that entire table highlighted. Once it's highlighted, I'm gonna go up to my Data tab. I'm gonna go over to What-If Analysis, and I'll go to Data Table. So, this will open up our Data Table window.

There's two options. Remember, I mentioned there's two different types of data tables. We're gonna utilize a single-variable data table, but there's also a multi-variable data table, and multi meaning two, where you can take two sets of variable values and plug them into a formula to get the results. Now, with ours, a single-variable data table, we've got a column of those alternate substitution values. So, I'm gonna go down to the Column Input cell.

We're gonna say, take these values right here, and input them into the C3 cell of this formula. So, for Column Input cell, I'm gonna grab C3. So, once again, taking each of these column values and plugging them into that spot so the formula can update. All right, you ready for this? I'm gonna hit Okay, and there's my results. We created the initial formula right there, and now we're just substituting those values in there to get the other results. This is an Excel single-variable data table. Try it out.

sections.title: Introduction to Python in Excel: From First Code Block to First Chart

lectures.title: Introduction to Python for Excel
lectures.text:
In this section, we're going to take a look at a relatively newer feature inside of Microsoft Excel where we can utilize Python inside of an Excel worksheet, specifically inside of a cell of a worksheet. Now I say cell because utilizing Python inside of Excel is much like using an Excel function. You start with equals, the Python function's called PY, you hit your Tab key, and you open up the Python editor where you can start to write your Python code.

Now, this first screenshot that I have here is just opening up the simple prompt equals PY, hit your Tab key, and you can now start to write your Python code inside of a cell. Now, your Python code can be really simple, such as just some simple math, like 10 plus two, and it'll return the results. Or it could be a little more involved where you're referencing data inside the Excel spreadsheet, such as a table, and then you can start to manipulate and summarize that data all through Python.

Now, this section is going to be purely an introduction into utilizing Python inside of Excel, but we are going to go through a number of topics. First, we'll talk about the basics of utilizing the PY function, really just getting it up and running, seeing a couple of simple commands in there just to get our feet wet and understanding of how Python is accessible through an Excel worksheet. Then we'll talk about creating a data frame, essentially referencing a table within your Excel worksheet all through Python.

We'll talk about making references to that data frame so you can start to manipulate it and get it to behave and represent what you're looking for. Then we'll talk about creating custom columns, new columns all through Python, creating calculations, grouping and summarizing your data frame data or your table data with Python, and being able to turn that summarized data into a visual such as a chart. So get ready. Let's jump in and start to work with Python inside of Excel.

And don't forget, attached to this lecture right here is a downloadable resource that you're going to want to download. Look for the Resources button, download the file, and open it up and follow along with me.

lectures.text:
As I mentioned in the earlier lecture, I love shortcut keys. Right, I can hit a button on my keyboard and get something to happen, whether that's a built-in shortcut keys in Excel, or shortcut keys that we assign to macros. But one of the downsides of shortcut keys is I've gotta remember 'em. I've gotta memorize all these different shortcut keys. I already have a hard enough time doing that just for my favorite commands inside of Excel. But now I gotta create macros and assign 'em shortcut keys to those, and then remember those, (hisses) I don't know, I don't know, right?

They're great, but you gotta remember 'em. You know, for me, I got little sticky notes, right? Reminding me of the favorite shortcut keys that I use, right? Or maybe you're sharing the file with somebody else and now they gotta remember the shortcut key. Well, there's other ways to run the macros as well, not just shortcut keys. Buttons are great, provide a nice little interface to be able to click on that would then activate and run your macro.

So we're gonna take a look at here at two different ways to create buttons inside the Excel interface. There's gonna be pros and cons of both options, and we'll talk about those as well. So first off, it's still inside the same workbook, InsertingAndformattingText. I'm gonna hop over to RUN WITH BUTTON worksheet, and here, I'm gonna place a button. I'm gonna place a button directly on the workbook. No, on the worksheet. To do that, I'll go to my Developer tab, top of the screen. And inside of there you got a section called Controls. It'll rerun the macro just like it did earlier. So let me try it out here. I'll give that button a click. You see I got kind of that little finger icon there. Give that a click. (fingers click) Done. The disadvantage to placing the button here, is the button is specific to the worksheet, right?

Now, for me personally, I've got two projects in there. I've got the Solver project. That's there because I activated the Solver add-in inside of Excel.

If you don't have the Solver, that's okay. You just don't have the Solver active inside of your copy of Excel. Maybe you had it earlier, maybe you deactivated it. Right below that, I've got my other VBA project, in this case, Book 1. This is in reference to my workbook, Book 1.

lectures.text:
Now that we've got a module inside of our Excel project, we can now create our very first VBA procedure. Now, inside of Excel VBA, you've got three different types of procedures you can create. For our purposes right now, and for most of this course, we're gonna be creating sub procedures, but there are two others and I'll give you a quick preview as to what those are as well. In our case, a sub procedure, it's much like the macro that we created earlier.

It just runs lines of code, just says, "I'm gonna do this and this and this and this." It just runs your code. And once it's done, it's done. It doesn't return any value, it just runs the code that you provide. Now to create a procedure, let's make sure that you're in module one. Once that's open, make sure you click into the module, then go to insert, and your first option there will be procedure. Now, a common question that I get at this point is sometimes procedure is not active, it's just grayed out.

Take a look. If I'm not actually clicked into the module, all I do is maybe just click on module one over here, and then I go to insert. You'll see that procedure is not active. If you go through the Q&A board of this course, that's a question that I get asked quite a bit. "How come procedure is not active for me?" Well, make sure you're in the module and you're literally clicked into the module. Then you'll have the option for procedure. So if I do that, insert procedure, I get my add procedure window, and my first step here is to give my procedure a name.

Now, if you watch the lecture on creating a macro, utilizing the macro recorder, the same concepts apply here. You remember all those keys? No spaces. You are gonna give your macro or you give your procedure a name, but you cannot have spaces in it. So I can say something like "fun with VBA procedures." There we go. No spaces. You can have numeric values in there, but you can't start it with the numeric value, and they can be up to 255 characters in length.

I would suggest don't use that. Try to keep your procedure names short to the point. Somebody could look at it and right away know what that procedure does. So same thing that applied to your macros. You give it a name. Once you've named it, you're then gonna specify the type of procedure. Like I mentioned, there's three of 'em. We're gonna deal with a sub procedure, the default one here. Sub-procedures, they just run your code. Boop, boop, boop, boop, top to bottom, starting with the first line in your procedure, runs it top to bottom.

Once it's done, it ends the procedure, and that procedure then goes away. The next one we have is what's called a function procedure. Now we're familiar with Excel functions, things like sum and min and max and count and V lookup and so on. You got all these built in functions. Functions, they're like sub-procedures where they run code, they perform some series of steps, but when they're done, they then return a value back to you. For example, the sum function.

You provided the range of cells, the Excel grabs those cells that then adds 'em up, and then it returns the result back to you. That's a function procedure. It'll perform some series of tasks, perhaps mathematical tasks, and then return a value back to you. The last one that we have here is a property procedure. Now we've talked about properties. Remember, Excel VBA is an object-oriented programming language. You get access to an object and then you get access to the properties that make up that object.

Well, here we can create properties of our own, which means we can also create objects of our own. You create an object, you can then create properties that deal with objects. So, so for our purposes in this course, we are primarily gonna deal with the subtype. We will see a function though, and we'll try out a function and see how that works as well. So for ours, we're gonna grab sub, and then we get the scope. The scope deals with where this procedure is gonna be available.

So by default it's called "public." That means that I can then reference and utilize this procedure anywhere within this Excel project. Remember, we're currently inside of this project right here, VBA Project Book 1. By making it public, if I create other modules and store code in those other modules or these other objects like the sheet one or this workbook, they all have access to utilizing this procedure because it's made public. If I mark it as private, right, the second option there, then this procedure is only available in the object it's created within.

In this case, it's only available to other code within module one. That's it. If I have module two or three or four or so on, I cannot make reference to this procedure 'cause it's private. Okay? All right. For us right now, we gave it a name, "fun with VBA procedures." It's gonna be up type sub, and we're gonna leave it marked as public. That's it. I'll hit okay, and I've now got the beginnings of my first VBA procedure. So let's get to this point.

We don't have any other code other than, "Hey, this is the name of our procedure. It's public, it's a sub procedure." And we're then gonna put all of our code inside of here. And when it's all done, it ends the sub and it's done. So let's get to that point, and then we'll start to write some of our own VBA code within that procedure.

lectures.text:
Here's a concept of programming in general, not just within VBA, but within any programming language that you pick up. Within your code, we should be adding comments, leave notes behind in the code. This is good for yourself. Give you an example here. I was working on a project where I wrote a whole bunch of scripts, and a year plus later, somebody came back to me and said, "Hey, I need some help here. I need to figure out why we're getting this bug.

Can you come over and take a look at this script that you wrote?" And I thought, oh wow, it's been a while. I'll see what I can do to help you out. lectures.title: Excel VBA MSGBOX Function
lectures.text:
We've talked about how Excel is built up of various objects. Through VBA, the programming, the object-oriented programming language, we can then communicate and manipulate those objects. Now, the objects that we've spoken about up to this point have been visual objects, objects that we can see within the Excel interface. Things we're already familiar with. Like the workbook, the worksheet, the sales, or the range. There are also objects that we don't see all the time.

They're not a part of just the default Excel interface. The first one that I want to talk about here is called a message box. This is already built into Excel. It's already there. We don't have to do a whole lot of programming to get it, but in order for us to see it, we have to make a call to it, we have to invoke the message box object. Now, a message box object is a way for us to provide a prompt to the user. We can give them a message. For example, if they run into an error while your code runs, we can give them a message box that comes up and tells them what went wrong.

Or perhaps we want to provide them with some additional information. When the macro first runs, you can provide them with a box that says, "Hey, this macro is about to do X, Y, and Z." Right, whatever it happens to be. But a prompting message to our users. So let's take a look at a message box. So we've got our FunWith procedures there, I'm just going to add to it. So I'm going to drop down one line, well, a couple of lines, below the ActiveSheet.Range("A1").Value = "Hello World".

So right below that, I'm going to create a reference to this message box object. So here, I'm just going to bring in msgbox. Now, again, this is built into the application, it's already there. And what I'm going to do is I'm going to provide a link to where you can find all the information through Microsoft about the msgbox, and I'll put that inside of the next lecture. So here, msgbox, if I now open up a parentheses, I now get a series of parameters or arguments that this message box needs in order to run.

Take a look. If this is all I do, right here, msgbox, open, close parentheses, call it good, I'll hit my Enter key. Uh-oh. Something is wrong. Expected = compile error. Well, that's not very descriptive for us. So, the problem here is, it's really not much going on here. I haven't given it any additional information other than I want get access to the message box. So let me delete out that close parentheses. I'm actually going to delete them both out and reopen the opening.

That way I can see the parameters once again. So there is one, two, three, four, five different parameters or arguments that the message box is looking for. You'll notice that number two, three, four, and five parameters are wrapped in square brackets. You see that bracket, Title, bracket, bracket, HelpFile, bracket, and so on? When you see an argument or parameter wrapped in those brackets, it means that it's optional, you don't have to use it.

In this case, the only one that is not is the prompt. So the prompt is required. So, bring that back. I'm going to bring in a prompt. And the prompt is really the message in the box. This is what you want to prompt the user with. So here, in quotes, I'm going to bring in Hello World again. And I'll close that quote, and I'll close the parentheses. So now I've got my message box, it's got a message in it, it's got a prompt. I'll hit my Enter key.

And now it let me pass. And you'll notice that it capitalized the M and the B. For me, personally, that lets me know that, oh, the Visual Basic Editor knew what that was. lectures.title: Cleaning Up the Final Report VBA Loop Code
lectures.text:
We're so close to wrapping up this procedure and making it perfect. Now, there's just a couple little things that we need to do here to make a little bit of tweaks to make sure that it's running smoothly with no hiccups. The first thing that we're gonna tweak here deals with our loop and the worksheets within that loop. Take a look. So in our main procedure, LoopYearlyReport, we've got our For Each loop that runs this set of commands right here.

Now, our loop goes For Each worksheet in the Worksheets collection. Now, in our Worksheets collection, it includes every worksheet in this workbook, which includes the Yearly Report. Now, I don't want our loop to go through the Yearly Report and copy and paste its content. That should only be happening on the East, West, North, and South worksheets, not on the Yearly Report. So we need to fix that right there, and this is something similar to what we did earlier, our solution.

If I get back into my Visual Basic window, I want the loop to go through, but I don't want any of this to take place if the active sheet is Yearly Report. So here, I'm just gonna bring in an If statement. I'm gonna say, "If worksheets," actually, not even worksheets. I'm just gonna say, 'If ws.Name does not equal "Yearly Report", then it can do all of this right here.' And I wanna make sure that down here at the bottom, right after the ActiveSheet.Paste, I End If.

Very important, very important. If you open the If, you gotta remember to close the If. You gotta End the If. I see people leave that off quite a bit, and it will throw an error. So what else I'm gonna do here is I'm gonna indent all of this just within the If. So if you highlight that and hit Tab on your keyboard, it'll indent it in. Not necessary, but so much easier to read. Now, it's clearly, this is the If, this is the condition, and if that's true, it'll do this right here.

So that's the first thing that we need to fix here, clean up the loop so that it won't run on the Yearly Report worksheet. Now, the next thing I wanna do here, just outside the If, so right below the 'Next ws,' once the loop is done, I then wanna make sure that I'm on the Yearly Report worksheet, which is gonna have just the raw data. Just the raw data, just all the records. It won't have the headers, it won't have the formatted headers, and it won't have the total column sum for us.

So I wanna perform those actions. So first, I'm gonna make sure that I am on the Yearly Report worksheet. So I'm gonna make sure that that one's selected, just utilizing the Worksheets object, reference the Yearly Report worksheet selected, and then I'm gonna run these three procedures right here: FormatHeaders, InsertHeaders, and AutomateTotalSum. That way, they get applied to the Yearly Report as well. Now, the AutomateTotalSum procedure, we created that one earlier, and it was all by itself.

It didn't have this main loop that we've now created utilizing the For Each, which does a whole bunch of other stuff. So if I scroll down to the AutomateTotalSum procedure, it has a loop of its own. And I don't want this thing to loop. I don't want the AutoSum to loop within itself. That's happening out here at the main procedure. So here, I'm gonna comment out the For Each line. I'm gonna comment out the 'Next ws.' Just put the single quotes, the apostrophes there.

And this line right here, 'Worksheets(ws.Name).Select,' we don't need that either. I could comment that out, because that is happening up here inside of the main procedure. So I don't need that to happen down here as well. You could comment 'em out like I'm doing. You could delete them out. We don't need those three lines, okay? In fact, if you leave them in there, our procedure's gonna get really wacky, 'cause it's gonna try to loop within itself.

Don't want that to happen. All right, so a little bit of cleanup. There's one more thing that we need to do here, but let's nail this down first. So bring in an If, make sure that this is not happening when Yearly Report is the active worksheet. Outside the loop, select the Yearly Report, run your three procedures, and remove the loop from the AutomateTotalSum procedure that we used earlier on. All right, get that done, and then there's one more tweak that we need to do here.

lectures.title: Adding Logic to Stop the Loop from Running Multiple Times on a Worksheet
lectures.text:
We've got one more tweak to our procedure, before everything is working perfectly. We're gonna walk through what's happening here, how we're gonna fix it, and then we'll implement it into our code. I'm gonna give you one solution to this problem that we're gonna see here, but there are many different ways that we can solve this solution and many different ways that we can code it here inside of VBA. So I want you to think about that. As we go through the solution that I'm gonna offer, think about what might be another way that you can do this as well.

So let's jump in and see what's happening here. So the problem that we're gonna see deals with the moment that we paste our content in. So think about this: Our loop runs. The first thing that happens is it goes to the east records worksheet. So if I hop over to east, it cleans the data up, it adds the headers, it calculates the data, and then it highlights the data copies, it goes to the yearly report, and then what happens? Let's get my VBA window back up here.

So we got the data copied, it goes to the worksheet, and then so that we can find the proper spot to paste the data, we have it drop all the way down at the bottom, A30,000 or some large number, and then it goes back up to find data. But the very first run through on this loop, there's no data on the worksheet. So this line right here tells it to go back up and it's gonna land inside a cell A1. Right there, A1. And then what do we tell it to do?

We tell it to offset one row, which moves it down to row two. In reality, I want the data to be inside of A1. I want Start inside a row one and then paste the data in. Well, the first time, because there's no data, it offsets down to an empty row down below A1. The second time, it'll jump up from a 30,000 jump up, find the data, and then offset down to the next empty row. So we're fine the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and so on, each time it goes through the loop, it's just the first time that causes the issue.

So here's a solution. We're gonna create essentially a little flag, and the first time our loop runs, the flag is gonna say, "This is the first time." That way the code knows, and the code can say, "Oh, it's the first time? Then I'm not gonna run the offset command. I'll just jump back up and I'll paste the data in." And then once it's run the first time, we'll then change that flag and say, "Oh, it's no longer the first time." So this time, as the loop goes through, it'll say, "Oh, okay, I'm no longer on the first time, I'm on the second or third or fourth time, it's okay to run the offset command here."

So here's our solution. Inside of our code, I'm gonna create a variable, and this variable's just gonna be called First Time. We talked about this earlier, but we never used it. The type is gonna be set to a Boolean type. This means it's a true/false data type. So the first time our code runs, we create the variable. Then we're going to initialize first time to be equal to true. It's the first time. So now with first time being equal to true, we'll come down to the offset command and we're gonna add some logic here.

I'm gonna bring in an if and say, if first time equals, well, let's say does not equal true, then we're gonna perform this operation right here. So if it's not equal to true, but it gets to this part, first time the loop runs, gets to this part, first time is equal to true, so it's check, "Hey, what's first time equal to? Is it not equal to true?" It's not, 'cause it is true. Then it skips over this part. But we need to change the flag. We need to say, "Hey, it's no longer the first time," so it's changed that to false.

So I'm gonna hop back into here and I'm gonna bring in an ELSE. And here we'll say first time equals false. It's no longer the first time. So the first time the loop runs, it checks the condition. Oh, that's not true. So skip this line. Jumps into the ELSE, changes that flag to false, and then carries on with the rest of the procedure. Then it loops back up, runs through everything inside the loop, gets back down here. First time is now equal to false, so it'll now run this line right here.

So this is one solution. Again, think about there's other ways that we can do this as well. I just want you to kind of brainstorm and think about what might be another solution. So I'll leave that up to you. Share any thoughts you have in the Q&A section of this course. So make sure you get this part here. Let's create the variable. Just call it First Time, it's gonna be a Boolean type. We'll initialize, we'll start that value being equal to true.

We'll create our condition, make sure that we also change that flag, change that variable to false, and we should be good to go. So let's get that part right there. Next lecture, we're gonna run this bad boy and let's see it work.
